standard_text: Interpret the equation y = mx + b as defining a linear function whose graph is a straight line; give examples of functions that are not linear. Describe similarities and differences between linear and nonlinear functions from tables, graphs, verbal descriptions, and equations.

progression.narrative: This standard asks students to read y = mx + b as a linear function whose graph is a straight line, to give examples of nonlinear functions, and to tell linear from nonlinear across equations, tables, graphs, and descriptions. The on-grade skills move from naming the slope and y-intercept to testing equations, graphs, and tables with one criterion: a constant rate of change. Students who stall here usually cannot read the coordinate plane fluently or do not see a table as a pattern with one per-step change. Intervention should rebuild grade 5 point plotting and grade 4 constant-change number patterns, then the grade 7 proportional relationship, where a table keeps one unit rate and its graph is a line through the origin. Once slope is felt as a unit rate, the linear versus nonlinear tests land.

steps.rationale: The definitional entry move: read y = mx + b and name m as the slope and b as the y-intercept. Every later comparison depends on knowing what the linear form looks like.
The standard says a linear function's graph is a straight line; this step makes the straight-line-vs-curve distinction explicit so 'linear' is tied to shape, not just to increasing.
Give and spot examples of nonlinear functions: decide from an equation whether it is linear (first-degree, no x in a denominator or exponent) or nonlinear (x^2, x^3, 1/x, 2^x).
Classify from a table, where the constant-rate criterion lives: linear exactly when equal x-steps give equal y-changes. This is where the 'it increases, so it's linear' misconception is settled.
The At-proficiency synthesis: compare functions presented in different representations at once (equation, table, graph, description) and decide which are linear using the properties of each form.
The Above-proficiency application: decide whether a real-world relationship is linear or nonlinear and justify it from the rate of change in the numbers.

skills.name: Plot and name points on the coordinate plane (first quadrant)

prerequisite_skill.description: Use an ordered pair (x, y) to plot a point: go right x units from the origin, then up y units. Name the ordered pair for a plotted point.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: To plot the point (3, 5), how far do you go right, and how far up?

skills.i_do_script: An ordered pair is a set of directions from the origin, and the order matters. Watch me plot (3, 5): I start at (0, 0), the corner where the axes cross. The first number is the x-coordinate, so I walk 3 units right along the x-axis. The second number is the y-coordinate, so I climb 5 units up. I land at one exact spot and mark it. If I flipped the numbers and went right 5 and up 3, I would land at (5, 3), a different point. Right first, then up, every time.

canonical_error.pattern: Reverses the coordinates, going up first and right second
canonical_error.example: Plots (3, 5) by going up 3 and right 5, landing on (5, 3) instead
canonical_error.why: The student is not tying the first number to the x-axis. The first coordinate always moves right along the x-axis and the second always moves up; swapping them lands on a different point.

skills.item_template: A first-quadrant grid with whole-number coordinates to 10. Student plots a point from an ordered pair, names the ordered pair for a marked point, or compares two points. Short response fluency bank.

sample_items.stem: To plot (3, 5), how many units do you go right, and how many up?
A point is 4 units right of the origin and 2 units up. What ordered pair names it?
In the ordered pair (2, 6), which number tells how far right to go?
What ordered pair names the origin?
Are (5, 1) and (1, 5) the same point?
sample_items.answer: No, the order matters; they are different points

sample_items.stem: You start at the origin, go right 6, and go up 0. What point are you on?
Which point is higher on the grid: (2, 7) or (7, 2)?
A point sits on the y-axis, 4 units up. What ordered pair names it?

redirect_script.stop: Which number goes with the x-axis?
redirect_script.prompt: Start at (0, 0). The first number is the walk right along the x-axis; the second number is the climb up. Say it as you move: right first, then up.
redirect_script.praise: You went right first and up second, so the pair landed you on the exact point.

vocabulary.definition: Two numbers (x, y) that locate a point: right x units, then up y units from the origin.
The point (0, 0), where the x-axis and y-axis cross.

next_steps.if_fail: Review grade 5 coordinate graphing with a labeled first-quadrant grid (right along x, then up along y).

worked_example_script.text: Draw a first-quadrant grid to 10. Put your pencil on the origin (0, 0).
To plot (3, 5), which way do you move first, and how far?
Right 3 along the x-axis, because the first number is the x-coordinate. Then up 5. Mark the point and label it (3, 5).
If a student goes up 3 first, have them plot both (3, 5) and (5, 3) and compare: two different points, so order matters.
Your turn: plot (4, 2) and (2, 4). Are they the same point?

skills.name: Extend a number pattern with a constant rule and find the amount of change

prerequisite_skill.description: Continue a number pattern that adds or subtracts the same amount each step, and name that amount.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: What number comes next in the pattern 2, 5, 8, 11?

skills.i_do_script: Some patterns grow by the same jump every time, and the jump is the rule. Watch 2, 5, 8, 11: from 2 to 5 is a jump of 3, from 5 to 8 is 3, from 8 to 11 is 3. Same jump every step, so the rule is add 3, and the next number is 11 + 3 = 14. On a number line I hop 3 each time and every hop is the same length. Some patterns do not have one jump: 2, 4, 8, 16 jumps by 2, then 4, then 8, so it has no single add rule. Find the jump first, then check that it repeats.

canonical_error.pattern: Extends the pattern without checking that the jump is the same, or names the wrong jump
canonical_error.example: For 2, 4, 8, 16 says the rule is add 2 and writes 18 next, checking only the first jump
canonical_error.why: The student tests one pair of neighbors and assumes the rule. A rule must hold between every pair; checking two or three jumps catches patterns that grow by changing amounts.

skills.item_template: A whole-number pattern of 4 or 5 terms that adds or subtracts a constant amount (or a non-example that does not). Student names the rule, the change, or the next term. Short response fluency bank.

sample_items.stem: What number comes next: 2, 5, 8, 11?
What is the rule for 6, 10, 14, 18?
How much does the pattern 9, 13, 17, 21 change each step?
What is the rule for 40, 35, 30, 25?
What number comes next: 50, 44, 38, 32?
A pattern starts at 3 and follows the rule add 6. Write the first four numbers.
Does the pattern 2, 4, 8, 16 add the same amount each step?
sample_items.answer: No, it jumps by 2, then 4, then 8

sample_items.stem: What number comes next: 7, 14, 21, 28?

redirect_script.stop: What is the jump between each pair of neighbors?
redirect_script.prompt: Subtract each number from the next one, pair by pair. If every jump is the same, that jump is the rule. Check at least two jumps before you extend.
redirect_script.praise: You checked every jump, so you know the rule really holds.

vocabulary.definition: The instruction a pattern follows, like add 3 or subtract 5.
One number in a pattern; terms come one after another in order.

next_steps.if_fail: Review grade 4 number patterns with number-line hops (a rule as one repeated jump).

worked_example_script.text: Draw a number line from 0 to 15. Mark 2, 5, 8, 11 and draw the hop from each mark to the next.
How long is each hop? Are all the hops the same length?
Every hop is 3, so the rule is add 3. One more hop from 11 lands on 14, the next term.
If a student writes the next term without measuring the hops, ask them to mark 2, 4, 8, 16 the same way: are those hops equal?
Your turn: mark 6, 10, 14, 18, name the rule, and find the next term.

skills.name: Decide from a table whether two quantities are proportional and find the unit rate

prerequisite_skill.description: Test whether a table is proportional by checking that y divided by x is the same for every row, and name that constant as the unit rate.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: A table shows 2 pounds cost 6 dollars and 5 pounds cost 15 dollars. Is the cost proportional to the weight?

skills.i_do_script: A table is proportional when every row shares one multiplier: y divided by x comes out the same every time. Watch x = 1, 2, 3 with y = 4, 8, 12: 4/1 = 4, 8/2 = 4, 12/3 = 4. One constant, 4, so the table is proportional and 4 is the unit rate, the amount of y for one x. Now watch x = 1, 2, 3 with y = 3, 5, 7: 3/1 = 3, but 5/2 = 2.5. The multiplier changed, so it is not proportional, even though y grows by the same 2 each row. Divide every row, then compare.

canonical_error.pattern: Calls a table proportional because y goes up by the same amount each row, checking differences instead of ratios
canonical_error.example: For x = 1, 2, 3 and y = 3, 5, 7 says proportional because y grows by 2 each time, missing that 3/1 and 5/2 are different
canonical_error.why: Equal differences make a pattern steady, but proportional needs equal ratios: one multiplier from x to y in every row. A table can climb by a constant amount and still not be proportional if it does not start from 0 at x = 0.

skills.item_template: A table of 3 or 4 whole-number rows (unit rates whole or half). Student decides proportional or not, or names the unit rate. MC or numeric response.

sample_items.stem: A table shows x = 1, 2, 3 and y = 4, 8, 12. Is y proportional to x?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Every ratio is 4; 'No' baits students who expect a trick when the check is clean.

sample_items.stem: A table shows x = 1, 2, 3 and y = 3, 5, 7. Is y proportional to x?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 'Yes' baits the equal-differences error: y grows by 2 each row, but 3/1 and 5/2 differ.

sample_items.stem: 3 pounds of apples cost 12 dollars at one steady price. What is the cost of 1 pound?
A table shows x = 2, 4, 6 and y = 5, 10, 15. What is the constant y divided by x?
In a proportional table, what must y be when x = 0?
Which table is proportional?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Only the first keeps one ratio (3). The others change ratio; the third climbs steadily by rows but its ratios are 4, 3, 2.5.

sample_items.stem: A table shows x = 4, 6, 10 and y = 10, 15, 25. Is it proportional, and if so what is the unit rate?
In the equation y = 5x, y is proportional to x. What is the unit rate?

redirect_script.stop: Did you divide, or did you subtract?
redirect_script.prompt: Proportional is a ratio test, not a difference test. Divide y by x in every row and compare. One shared answer means proportional, and that answer is the unit rate.
redirect_script.praise: You divided every row and compared the ratios, that is the proportional test.

vocabulary.definition: A relationship where y is always the same multiple of x, so y divided by x never changes.
The amount of y for exactly one x; the constant you get from y divided by x.
The one multiplier k in y = kx; it equals the unit rate.

worked_example_script.text: Write the table x = 2, 3, 5 with y = 8, 12, 20. Add a third column labeled y divided by x.
Fill the new column. What do you get for each row?
8/2 = 4, 12/3 = 4, 20/5 = 4. One constant, so the table is proportional and the unit rate is 4: every 1 of x brings 4 of y.
If a student subtracts rows instead, point at the column: the test is division, one multiplier for every row.
Your turn: test x = 1, 2, 3 with y = 3, 5, 7 the same way. Proportional or not?

practice_problems.stem: 2 tickets cost 8 dollars at one steady price. What does 1 ticket cost?
practice_problems.answer: 4 dollars

practice_problems.stem: If x = 3 and y = 12, what is y divided by x?
A table shows x = 1, 2, 5 and y = 6, 12, 30. Is y proportional to x? Name the unit rate if so.
practice_problems.answer: Yes, every ratio is 6, so the unit rate is 6

practice_problems.stem: A table shows x = 2, 3, 4 and y = 7, 9, 11. Is y proportional to x?
practice_problems.answer: No. The differences are equal (2 each) but the ratios are 3.5, 3, and 2.75, so there is no single multiplier

practice_problems.stem: A proportional table has unit rate 2.5. What is y when x = 6?
A table shows x = 4, 8, 12 and y = 6, 12, 18. What is the constant of proportionality?
A proportional table shows x = 5 with y = 20, and one more row with y = 32. What is x in that row?
practice_problems.answer: 8, because the unit rate is 4 and 32 divided by 4 is 8

practice_problems.stem: Marco tested the table x = 1, 2, 3 with y = 4, 6, 8. Find his mistake and fix it.
practice_problems.answer: He checked differences, not ratios. 4/1 = 4 but 6/2 = 3, so the multiplier changes and the table is not proportional.

activities.title: One Multiplier or Many?
activities.instructions:
1. Build the row x = 1 for the rate 3 per 1: one cube on the left, three counters on the right.
2. Build x = 2 and x = 3 the same way and record the table 1 to 3, 2 to 6, 3 to 9.
3. For each row, say the multiplier out loud: 3 counters for every cube.
4. Now build 1 to 3, 2 to 5, 3 to 7 and try to say one multiplier for every row. It breaks at row two.
5. Write the claim: proportional means one multiplier works for every row.

activities.title: Proportional or Not?
activities.instructions:
1. Spread the table cards face up.
2. For each card, write y divided by x beside every row, then sort into Proportional and Not Proportional.
3. To place a card in Proportional, say its unit rate out loud.
4. Two cards climb by equal differences but are not proportional; explain why they fail the ratio test.

strategy_links.why: Cubes and counters make 'one multiplier for every row' visible before the divide-and-compare procedure is named.
The equal-differences-so-proportional error is stable; finding and fixing it in a worked table confronts it directly.
Thinking aloud 'divide, then compare' keeps the ratio test in front of the subtraction habit.

questioning_prompts: What is y divided by x in this row? And in the next row?
Is your check a subtraction or a division? Which one tests proportional?
What does the unit rate tell you about one single x?
A table climbs by 2 every row. Is that enough to call it proportional?
What must the table show at x = 0 if it is proportional?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student calls a table proportional because the y values climb by equal amounts.
misconception_redirects.say: Equal jumps is a pattern test, not the proportional test. Divide y by x in every row: do you get one shared multiplier?
misconception_redirects.praise: You switched from subtracting to dividing, that is the right test.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student divides only the first row and stops.
misconception_redirects.say: One row cannot show a constant. Divide every row, then compare all the answers before you decide.
misconception_redirects.praise: You checked every row, so your yes actually means proportional.

quick_checks.look_for: Yes, every ratio is 2.5. A no usually means the student subtracted rows.
No, the ratios change. A yes diagnoses the equal-differences error.

worked_solution.stem: A table shows x = 2, 3, 5 and y = 8, 12, 20. Is y proportional to x? If so, name the unit rate.

steps.annotation: Divide y by x in the first row.
Divide in the second row and compare.
Divide in the last row; all three ratios match.
One shared multiplier means proportional, and 4 is the amount of y for one x.

faded_example.stem: A table shows x = 2, 4, 5 and y = 6, 12, 15. Is y proportional to x? If so, name the unit rate.

steps.annotation: Divide y by x in the first row.
Divide in the second row and compare.
Divide in the last row and compare all three ratios.
State proportional or not, and name the unit rate.

sentence_starters: I divided y by x in every row and got ___, so the table is ___.
The unit rate is ___ because every 1 of x brings ___ of y.
The jumps are equal but the ratios are ___, so it is not proportional.

skills.name: Identify the unit rate from the graph of a proportional relationship

prerequisite_skill.description: Recognize that a proportional relationship graphs as a straight line through the origin, and read the unit rate as the y value at x = 1.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: A proportional graph passes through the origin and the point (1, 4). What is the unit rate?

skills.i_do_script: A proportional relationship makes the plainest graph in mathematics: a straight line through the origin. Watch y = 3x: at x = 0 it gives 0, at x = 1 it gives 3, at x = 2 it gives 6. I plot (0, 0), (1, 3), (2, 6) and they line up straight from the corner. The unit rate hides at x = 1: the point (1, 3) says one x brings 3 y, so the unit rate is 3. If the line misses the origin, like one through (0, 2), it is not proportional, because zero x should bring zero y. Find the origin, then read the height at x = 1.

canonical_error.pattern: Reads the unit rate from the wrong point, or accepts a line that misses the origin as proportional
canonical_error.example: For a line through (0, 0) and (2, 6) says the unit rate is 6 because 6 is the y value they see, instead of 6/2 = 3; or calls a line through (0, 2) proportional because it is straight
canonical_error.why: The unit rate is y for exactly one x. At any other point you must divide y by x to get back to one. And straight alone is not enough: a proportional line must also pass through the origin, since zero of x brings zero of y.

skills.item_template: A first-quadrant line through the origin, described by two labeled points (whole or half unit rates). Student names the unit rate, tests a point, or decides whether the graph shows a proportional relationship. MC or numeric response.

sample_items.stem: A proportional graph passes through the origin and (1, 4). What is the unit rate?
A proportional graph passes through the origin and (2, 6). What is the unit rate?
A straight line crosses the y-axis at (0, 2). Can it show a proportional relationship?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 'Yes' baits students who think straight is the whole test; proportional also requires passing through the origin.

sample_items.stem: On the graph of a proportional relationship, which point shows the unit rate directly?
sample_items.answer: The point at x = 1, that is (1, unit rate)

sample_items.stem: A proportional graph passes through (4, 10). What is the unit rate?
Line A passes through the origin and (1, 5). Line B passes through the origin and (1, 3). Which line is steeper?
sample_items.distractor_logic: A larger unit rate means a steeper line; 'Line B' baits reading the smaller number as steeper.

sample_items.stem: A graph shows y = 2x. Name three points on the line, starting at the origin.
A proportional graph has unit rate 5. What is y at x = 3?

redirect_script.stop: Does the line pass through the origin, and what is its height at x = 1?
redirect_script.prompt: Check the origin first: proportional lines start at (0, 0). Then read the y value directly above x = 1; that height is the unit rate. From any other point, divide y by x to get back to one.
redirect_script.praise: You checked the origin and read the height at x = 1, that is exactly how the graph shows the rate.

vocabulary.definition: The point (0, 0); every proportional graph passes through it because zero of x brings zero of y.
The y value at x = 1 on a proportional graph; how much y one unit of x brings.
How fast a line climbs; a larger unit rate makes a steeper proportional line.

worked_example_script.text: On a first-quadrant grid, plot (0, 0), (1, 3), and (2, 6), then draw the straight line through them.
Where does the line start? What is its height directly above x = 1?
It starts at the origin and stands 3 tall at x = 1, so the unit rate is 3: every 1 across brings 3 up. The point (2, 6) agrees, since 6 divided by 2 is also 3.
If a student calls the unit rate 6 from the point (2, 6), walk them back to x = 1: the rate is y for ONE x.
Your turn: a proportional line passes through (2, 8). Plot it and name the unit rate.

practice_problems.stem: A proportional graph passes through the origin and (1, 2). What is the unit rate?
Every proportional graph passes through which point?
practice_problems.answer: The origin, (0, 0)

practice_problems.stem: A proportional graph passes through (3, 12). What is the unit rate, and what point sits at x = 1?
practice_problems.answer: The unit rate is 4, and the point is (1, 4)

practice_problems.stem: A straight line passes through (0, 3) and (1, 5). Is it a proportional relationship?
practice_problems.answer: No, it misses the origin, so zero x does not give zero y

practice_problems.stem: Line A goes through the origin and (1, 6); line B goes through the origin and (2, 8). Which is steeper?
practice_problems.answer: Line A, its unit rate is 6 and line B's is 4

practice_problems.stem: A proportional graph has unit rate 2.5. Name the points on the line at x = 0, x = 2, and x = 4.
A proportional line passes through (5, 10) and one other labeled point (x, 6). What is x?
practice_problems.answer: 3, because the unit rate is 2 and 6 divided by 2 is 3

practice_problems.stem: Lena read a proportional graph through the origin and (2, 6). Find her mistake and fix it.
practice_problems.answer: She read y at x = 2, but the unit rate is y for one x. Divide: 6/2 = 3, so the unit rate is 3 and the point at x = 1 is (1, 3).

activities.title: Climb the Rate
activities.instructions:
1. Both partners plot (0, 0). One builds the rate 3 per 1: from each point, go right 1 and up 3, marking (1, 3), (2, 6), (3, 9). The other builds 2 per 1: (1, 2), (2, 4), (3, 6).
2. Draw both lines and compare: which is steeper, and which unit rate is larger?
3. Circle each line's point at x = 1 and label it 'unit rate lives here.'
4. Check a far point on each line by dividing y by x; say why it matches the height at x = 1.

activities.title: Point, Rate, Line
materials: Card deck: point cards, unit rate cards
activities.instructions:
1. Spread the cards face up.
2. Match each point card, a labeled point on a proportional line through the origin, to its unit rate card.
3. To claim a match, say the division out loud, like 6 divided by 2 is 3.
4. One decoy point card sits on a line that misses the origin; set it aside and explain why it has no unit rate match.

strategy_links.why: Building the line hop by hop, right 1 and up the rate, makes steepness a physical count before it becomes slope.
Comparing two origin lines with different unit rates makes 'bigger rate, steeper line' explicit.
Reading the rate from a point other than x = 1 is a precise error a find-and-fix names cleanly.

questioning_prompts: Does this line pass through the origin? Why must a proportional line do that?
What is the y value directly above x = 1?
The labeled point is (2, 6). How do you get the unit rate from it?
Which of these two lines is steeper, and which unit rate is bigger?
If the unit rate is 4, what point must the line hit at x = 3?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student reads the y value of any labeled point as the unit rate.
misconception_redirects.say: The unit rate is y for exactly one x. At (2, 6) you have two x's worth, so divide: 6/2 = 3. Walk back to x = 1 and check the height.
misconception_redirects.praise: You divided back to one x, that is the unit rate.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student calls any straight line proportional.
misconception_redirects.say: Straight is only half the test. Check the origin: zero of x must bring zero of y. A line starting at (0, 2) is straight but not proportional.
misconception_redirects.praise: You checked the origin, not just the straightness.

quick_checks.prompt: A proportional graph passes through (2, 10). What is the unit rate?
quick_checks.look_for: 5, from 10 divided by 2. An answer of 10 means the student read the point instead of dividing to one x.

quick_checks.prompt: A straight line starts at (0, 4). Proportional?
quick_checks.look_for: No, it misses the origin. A yes means straightness is being used as the whole test.

worked_solution.stem: A proportional graph passes through the origin and the labeled point (2, 8). What is the unit rate?

steps.annotation: Confirm the origin first; that is what makes it proportional.
This point shows 8 of y for 2 of x, not for 1.
Divide y by x to get the amount for one x.
The line stands 4 tall at x = 1.

faded_example.stem: A proportional graph passes through the origin and the labeled point (3, 12). What is the unit rate?

steps.annotation: Confirm the origin first.
This shows 12 of y for 3 of x.
Divide y by x to get the amount for one x.
State the unit rate and the point at x = 1.

sentence_starters: The line passes through the origin, so the relationship is ___.
At x = 1 the line stands ___ tall, so the unit rate is ___.
From the point (___, ___) I divided and got a unit rate of ___.

skills.name: Identify the slope and y-intercept from an equation in y = mx + b form
skills.i_do_script: The two numbers in y = mx + b each DO something, and a table catches them in the act. Tabulate y = 2x + 3 at x = 0, 1, 2, 3: y = 3, 5, 7, 9. The 3 shows up immediately -- it's the value at x = 0, where the line starts. The 2 shows up between every pair of rows -- each step of 1 in x jumps y by 2. So m is the per-step jump (the slope) and b is the row-zero start (the y-intercept). That's why m sits WITH the x -- it gets applied for every unit of x -- and b stands alone -- it happens once, before any x. Watch y = 6x - 4: the 6 is the jump per step, the -4 is the start (carry the sign). Position is the shortcut; the jobs are the meaning.

canonical_error.pattern: Swaps m and b -- names the constant as the slope and the coefficient of x as the y-intercept
canonical_error.example: For y = 2x + 3, says the slope is 3 and the y-intercept is 2, reading the standalone number as the slope
canonical_error.why: The student is not tying m to the number multiplied by x. In y = mx + b the slope is the coefficient of x and the y-intercept is the constant; swapping them mislabels the whole line.

skills.item_template: A linear equation in y = mx + b form (b != 0). Student identifies the slope and/or the y-intercept. Short response / dropdown.

sample_items.stem: In the equation y = mx + b, what does m represent?
In the equation y = mx + b, what does b represent?
Identify the slope and the y-intercept of y = 2x + 3.
Identify the slope and the y-intercept of y = -5x + 7.
What is the y-intercept of y = 4x - 9?

redirect_script.stop: Which number is multiplied by x?
redirect_script.prompt: Build the table at x = 0, 1, 2: which number appears at x = 0, and which number is the jump between rows? The jump is the slope; the x = 0 value is the intercept.
redirect_script.praise: You matched m to the number with x (slope) and b to the lonely number (y-intercept) -- exactly the form.

vocabulary.definition: The constant rate of change of a line; the value m (the coefficient of x) in y = mx + b.
Where the line crosses the y-axis; the value b (the constant term) in y = mx + b.
A linear equation written as y = mx + b, with the slope and y-intercept shown directly.

worked_example_script.text: Tabulate y = 2x + 3 at x = 0, 1, 2, 3 and plot the points: (0,3), (1,5), (2,7), (3,9).
Where does the 3 from the equation show up in the table -- which row? And the 2 -- what happens between every pair of rows?
The 3 is the value at x = 0 (the start); the 2 is the jump y makes for each step of 1 in x. m is the per-step jump, b is the row-zero start -- 'the number with the x' is just where the jump lives.
Write 'y = 6x - 4. Identify the slope and the y-intercept.'
Which number is multiplied by x, and which stands alone?
6 is with the x, so the slope is 6. -4 stands alone, so the y-intercept is -4 -- keep the minus sign.
If a student says the slope is -4, ask 'is the -4 attached to the x, or is the 6?'
Your turn: for y = -3x + 8, name the slope and the y-intercept.

practice_problems.stem: In y = mx + b, which letter is the slope?
practice_problems.answer: m

practice_problems.stem: In y = 5x + 2, which number is multiplied by x?
practice_problems.answer: 5 (the slope)

practice_problems.stem: Identify the slope and the y-intercept of y = 2x + 3.

skills.name: Recognize that a linear function graphs as a straight line and a nonlinear function graphs as a curve
skills.i_do_script: The standard says a linear function's graph is a straight line. So the test for a graph is simple: is it a straight line, or does it bend into a curve? A straight line has the same steepness the whole way -- a constant rate of change. A curve gets steeper or flatter as it goes. Watch a graph through (0,1), (1,4), (2,7), (3,10): each step across raises it the same 3, so it never bends -- a straight line, linear. A graph through (0,0), (1,1), (2,4), (3,9) rises by 1, then 3, then 5 -- it steepens, so it curves -- nonlinear. The trap is thinking 'it goes up, so it's linear.' A curve goes up too.

canonical_error.why: The student equates 'increasing' with 'linear.' Linear requires a STRAIGHT line -- the same steepness throughout; a curve rises with a changing steepness, so rising alone doesn't make it linear.

skills.name: Classify an equation as linear or nonlinear
skills.i_do_script: A straight line climbs by the same amount every single step -- and only one thing produces that steady climb: multiplying x by a fixed number and adding a constant. The moment x gets squared or dropped into a denominator, the steps stop being equal and the graph bends. An equation is linear only when x appears to the first power -- just plain x, no exponent, and never in a denominator or as a power. That is the y = mx + b family. Watch four equations: y = -4x + 1 is linear (plain x). y = x^2 + 2 is nonlinear (x is squared). y = 1/x + 3 is nonlinear (x is in the bottom of a fraction). y = 10x^2 + 5 is nonlinear (x squared again). Only y = -4x + 1 is a straight line. The signal to hunt for is anything happening to x besides multiplying by a number and adding a constant.

canonical_error.pattern: Calls a nonlinear equation linear because it 'has an x' or 'looks like an equation,' ignoring the exponent or the x in the denominator
canonical_error.example: Says y = 1/x + 3 is linear because it has +3 and a single x, missing that x is in the denominator (nonlinear); or calls y = x^2 + 2 linear because it has no visible number in front
canonical_error.why: The student checks only for the presence of x, not for what is done to it. Linear needs x to the first power with no x in a denominator or exponent; an x^2, x^3, 1/x, or 2^x breaks the linear form.

skills.name: Determine whether a table represents a linear or nonlinear function
skills.i_do_script: A table is linear exactly when it has a constant rate of change: for equal steps in x, y changes by the same amount every time. skills.name: Compare functions in different representations and identify which are linear
skills.i_do_script: The same linear test works in every representation, and I apply the right check for each form. For an equation, x must be to the first power. For a table, the y-changes must be equal for equal x-steps. For a graph, it must be a straight line. For a description, the same amount must be added each step. canonical_error.why: The student uses a single surface cue across all forms. Each representation needs its own linear check: first-power x (equation), equal y-changes (table), straight line (graph), constant amount added (description).

skills.name: Determine and justify whether a real-world relationship is linear or nonlinear
skills.i_do_script: In a real-world situation I decide linear or nonlinear by checking the rate of change in the numbers, then I justify it. Watch a hexagon: as the side length grows by 1, the perimeter grows by 6 each time -- a constant rate -- so the relationship is linear. Now a town's population: it goes up by 200, then 250, then 300 -- it keeps increasing, but by a DIFFERENT amount each year, so the rate varies and the relationship is nonlinear. The justification names the constant-or-changing rate, not just 'it goes up.'

canonical_error.pattern: Calls a real-world relationship linear because a quantity keeps increasing, without checking whether it increases by a constant amount
canonical_error.example: For a town population that rises by 200, then 250, then 300 each year, says 'linear because the population goes up every year'
canonical_error.why: The student treats any steady growth as linear. Linear requires a CONSTANT rate -- the same increase each equal step; a quantity can rise every step while the amount of increase keeps changing (nonlinear).

skills.item_template: A real-world situation as a table or description. Student decides linear or nonlinear and justifies from the rate of change. Multi-part / short response. Tables as data_table.

sample_items.stem: The table shows a regular hexagon's side length and its perimeter. Is the relationship linear or nonlinear? Justify your answer.
sample_items.answer: Linear. The perimeter increases by a constant 6 for each 1-unit increase in side length (a constant rate of change).

sample_items.stem: A town's population is recorded each year. Is the relationship between the year and the population linear or nonlinear? Justify your answer.
sample_items.answer: Nonlinear. The population rises by 200, then 250, then 300 -- it increases every year, but by a different amount each time, so the rate of change is not constant.

sample_items.stem: The table shows a square's side length and its area. Is the relationship linear or nonlinear? Justify your answer.
sample_items.answer: Nonlinear. The area increases by 3, then 5, then 7, then 9 -- the rate of change grows, so it is not constant (this is area = side^2).

sample_items.stem: A worker earns a fixed hourly wage. The table shows hours worked and total pay. Is the relationship linear or nonlinear? Justify your answer.
sample_items.answer: Linear. Pay increases by a constant $9 for each additional hour -- a constant rate of change.

diagnostic_flow.description: Start with S3, classifying an equation as linear or nonlinear, the clean grade-level discriminator. If they pass, move up to S4 (classify a table) and S5 (compare across representations). If they fail, drop below grade level: B1 checks whether a table is proportional with one unit rate, and B2 checks reading the unit rate from a line through the origin, the two grade 7 skills that slope and constant rate lean on. If those wobble, the foundations F1 (plotting points, grade 5) and F2 (constant-change number patterns, grade 4) locate the gap. S1 and S2 remain available to probe the standard's own slope-intercept and straight-line-versus-curve groundwork, and S6 stays as the real-world synthesis check.
